title: Vayetze: the stone on the well (Genesis 29:9–11)
hookLine: Jacob rolls away a stone meant for many shepherds, then weeps

lines: A YOUNG WOMAN WITH HER SHEEP.
cards: You've heard the stories. A mother lifts a car off her child. A tired dad carries a sleeping kid up three flights of stairs without noticing.
Love does strange things to a body. Jacob, after weeks on the road, comes to a well in a field in the east. Three flocks of sheep lie beside it, waiting.
On the well's mouth sits a great stone, so heavy, the shepherds tell him, that they can only move it when all the shepherds gather. Then a young woman walks up with her father's sheep.

teach.b: Jacob asks the shepherds why they're waiting. It's the middle of the day: water the sheep and go back to pasture.
We can't, they say, not until all the flocks are gathered and together we roll the stone from the well's mouth. That's the rule of this well. It takes everyone.
While they're still talking, Rachel arrives, the daughter of Laban, his mother's brother.
She's a shepherd, the text says; she tends her father's flock herself. Jacob sees her.

He goes up, alone, and rolls the stone off the mouth of the well, the stone that took all the shepherds together. Rashi says he moved it as easily as pulling a cork from a bottle, to show how strong he was.
He waters his uncle's whole flock. And then, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Jacob kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice, and wept."
Why weep, at the happiest moment? The text doesn't say. The rabbis offered answers.

teach.h: AND JACOB KISSED RACHEL, AND WEPT.
teach.b: One midrash says he wept because he came empty-handed: his grandfather's servant had arrived at a well like this one with ten camels loaded with gifts, and Jacob had nothing to give.
Rashi also says he foresaw that Rachel would not be buried beside him. Maybe it was just everything at once: the road, the fear, the relief of family, love at first sight.
Strength and tears in the same scene, and the Torah doesn't make him choose. Love made him strong enough to move a stone meant for many, and soft enough to cry in front of strangers.

how: Jacob and Rachel's meeting at the well is read each late autumn in Vayetze, and the well is a recurring meeting place in the Torah's love stories, from Rebekah to Rachel to Moses and Zipporah.

o: and he labored, Jacob's years of work
and he loved, Jacob meeting Rachel
and he went out, Jacob's road from home

games.q: who did what at the well — tap the pairs.

games.q: you've traveled for weeks. at a well, the shepherds say the stone needs all of them. then Rachel arrives. you're Jacob. what do you do?
o: ask Rachel to fetch her father.
games.why: Jacob rolled the stone off alone, watered her flock, kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice and wept.

practice: Think of one stone in your life right now, something that feels too heavy for you alone: a task, a conversation, a long week.
Then think of someone you love, and why you'd want to do it for them, and feel whether the stone gets any lighter. If some tears come with it, let them; Jacob had both.

wordCard.voice: Vayetze. And he went out: the portion where Jacob, alone, rolls a stone meant for many, for Rachel, and then weeps.

carryVoice: Your line: love moves stones. And it leaves room for tears. Day one hundred ninety-four, done.
